evidence_items.claim: Symeon or Simon names the sender within the letter; neither reading by itself proves or disproves direct Petrine authorship.
Slave and apostle are paired self-designations, but later office or authority theories should not be imported without argument.
The transfiguration appeal contrasts eyewitness testimony with devised myths inside the rhetoric; it does not make every later apostolic claim self-authenticating.
The majestic glory is the source of the heavenly voice in the narrative; proposals about the phrase's Jewish liturgical or apocalyptic background are comparative.
The morning star may mark eschatological illumination, Christ, or inward confirmation; the metaphor should remain open where the syntax is contested.

Prophecy of Scripture and private interpretation concerns prophecy's origin or interpretation in context; it cannot simply prohibit study, questions, translation, or accountable communal disagreement.
Prophecy being carried by the Spirit grounds divine agency but does not by itself define dictation, inerrancy, a closed canon, or a modern prophetic office.
Prophecy must be tested through context, evidence, and accountable community; appeals to this passage must not enable manipulation, anti-intellectualism, secrecy, or leader immunity.
Faith of equal honor resists status hierarchy in the prescript; its precise comparison group remains grammatically and socially debated.
Divine power and precious promises ground the exhortation; the text does not promise health, wealth, control, or exemption from ordinary care.
Participation in divine nature has moral and eschatological context and has supported theosis traditions; it does not erase creaturely difference or authorize spiritual elites.

Application must reject antisemitism, supersessionism, opponent dehumanization, misogyny, anti-LGBTQ coercion, nationalism, colonial mission, forced conversion, religious violence, prosperity extraction, and ecological neglect.
The virtue sequence is cumulative rhetoric, not a validated psychological stage model or basis for ranking persons by worth or ability.
Confirming calling and election is an exhortation to practiced fidelity; traditions disagree about assurance, merit, perseverance, and apostasy.
Entrance into the eternal kingdom is promised rhetorically to encourage diligence, not to support commodified merit or leader-controlled access.
Memory and reminder organize the letter and fit farewell-testament convention; genre comparison does not settle historical authorship.
Tent and exodus signify approaching death and may echo transfiguration tradition; exact source, chronology, and autobiographical force remain disputed.
The promises are said to make the addressees participants in divine nature after escape from corrupt desire.
The letter attributes everything for life and godliness to divine power through knowledge.
The audience is exhorted to make its calling and election firm through diligent practice.
The addressees are described as receiving faith of equal honor with the sender's group.
Repeated reminder is a stated purpose of the letter.
The letter says no prophecy of Scripture comes from idias epilyseos.
The prophetic word is likened to a lamp shining in a dark place until day dawns and a morning star rises.
The prescript names Symeon or Simon Peter as slave and apostle of Jesus Christ.
Prophetic speech is attributed to people speaking from God while carried by the Holy Spirit.
The named sender depicts approaching death as putting aside a tent and as exodus.
The letter presents plural eyewitnesses hearing a heavenly voice about Jesus on a holy mountain.
Faith, excellence, knowledge, self-control, endurance, godliness, mutual affection, and love form a literary sequence.
Prophetic oracles use treaty, courtroom, and royal imagery familiar in the ancient world, but they do so to speak for the LORD.
The prophets address real crises in Israel, Judah, and the nations, speaking to covenant breach and coming judgment or restoration.
Ancient collections often guided interpretation by arrangement, and Scripture similarly invites readers to move from promise to fulfillment.
This approach grows from the church's long habit of reading Scripture as a unified canon rather than isolated fragments.
